name: Milne Universe
description: Edward Arthur Milne's expanding universe of 1932: test particles flying apart from one event of flat spacetime with every speed below that of light. In comoving coordinates it is the empty open Friedmann universe, with scale factor $ct$ and hyperbolic space at each moment.
history: Edwin Hubble found in 1929 that the nebulae recede with velocities in proportion to their distances [hubble1929]. In July 1932 the "most commonly accepted explanation" of it, as Edward Arthur Milne put it, was the expanding curved space of Alexander Friedmann and Georges Lemaître [milne1932, friedmann1922, lemaitre1927]. Milne, born at Hull in 1896, set out to explain the recession with no gravitation and in flat, static Euclidean space [mccrea1951, milne1933]. He published a summary on 2 July 1932 and finished the full account, 95 pages, at the Einstein Institute in Potsdam in November [milne1932, milne1933]. He pictured a swarm of particles leaving one event in straight lines with every speed below that of light, so that at the time $t$ after it every particle sees every other recede at $r/t$, where $r$ is its distance [milne1933].¶Milne took the kinematics of Einstein's special relativity whole and added one postulate: "not only the laws of nature, but also the events occurring in nature, the world itself, must appear the same to all observers" [milne1933]. The swarm then fills a sphere about any one of its particles whose edge recedes at the speed of light, and the world is, in his words, "perfectly ego-centric at all points" [milne1933]. He first called the postulate the extended principle of relativity, and by July 1933 he was writing of it as the cosmological principle [milne1933, milne1933note].¶Howard Percy Robertson, and independently William Ogilvy Kermack and William Hunter McCrea, showed in 1933 that Milne's swarm is a limiting case of relativistic cosmology, the limit in which the density tends to zero [robertson1933, kermack1933, milne1933remarks]. Robertson wrote Minkowski spacetime inside the light cone of one event in the coordinates of particles moving out from it, and recognised the line element as the special case $R = c\tau$, $k = -1$ of the one relativistic cosmology is built on, with the effect of matter on it negligible [robertson1933]. It is the open Friedmann universe with no matter in it, its space of constant negative curvature, of the kind Friedmann had admitted in 1924 [robertson1933, friedmann1924]. Milne answered in June 1933 that those who describe particles at rest in expanding space of constant negative curvature "are at bottom only discussing moving particles in flat space" [milne1933remarks].¶In 1934 Milne, and McCrea with him, worked out in Newtonian mechanics the expansion of a uniform cloud of dust [milne1934, mccrea1934, mukhanov2005]. Milne built his ideas into a kinematic relativity, set out in his book of 1935 [milne1935]. Robertson in 1935 and Arthur Geoffrey Walker in 1937 turned the demand that the world look the same to every one of its observers into a derivation of the homogeneous and isotropic line element from kinematics alone, and that line element carries their names [robertson1935, walker1937, ellis2012]. Robertson found in the same work that Milne's own conditions pick out the expansion $\xi(\tau) = \tau$ with $k = -1$ [robertson1935]. Herbert Dingle attacked Milne's method in May 1937 under the title "Modern Aristotelianism" [dingle1937]. Milne answered him on 12 June, beside replies from Arthur Eddington, Paul Dirac, McCrea and eleven others, and Dingle answered them all [milne1937, dingle1937reply].¶The Milne universe is the region $cT > R$ of Minkowski spacetime inside the future light cone of one event, in the coordinates of the particles moving out from it, and its Riemann tensor vanishes [robertson1933, mukhanov2005]. Viatcheslav Mukhanov describes it as "simply a piece of Minkowski spacetime described in expanding coordinates", with space of curvature $k = -1$ and a spacetime of zero curvature [mukhanov2005]. Wolfgang Rindler showed in 1956 that Milne's model has neither an event horizon nor a particle horizon [rindler1956]. An open universe of matter comes to be dominated by its negative spatial curvature as it expands, and then expands as the Milne universe does, with $a \propto t$ [barrow2002].¶Nicholas Birrell and Paul Davies used the Milne universe in 1982 to show the role adiabaticity plays in judging whether a quantum state of a field in an expanding universe is physically reasonable [birrell1982]. Justin Khoury, Burt Ovrut, Nathan Seiberg, Paul Steinhardt and Neil Turok modelled a big crunch followed by a big bang in 2002 on a two dimensional Milne universe compactified by a boost, in which the distance between two branes is proportional to $|t|$ and vanishes as they collide [khoury2002]. Turok, Malcolm Perry and Steinhardt took the same compactified Milne spacetime as the background in which two empty orbifold planes of M theory collide at constant speed [turok2004]. Aurélien Benoit-Lévy and Gabriel Chardin proposed in 2012 a universe of matter and antimatter, the antimatter with negative active gravitational mass, whose scale factor grows linearly with time, as the Milne universe's does [benoitlevy2012].

coordinates.name: Comoving Hyperbolic
coordinates.convention: We use the cosmic time $t$, the proper time of each comoving particle since the event $t = 0$, and the hyperbolic angle $\chi$, the rapidity of a comoving particle relative to the one at $\chi = 0$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Comoving Spherical
coordinates.convention: We use the cosmic time $t$ and the comoving radius $r = \sinh\chi$, a pure number, the areal radius of the sphere through a point divided by $ct$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Logarithmic Time

parameters.description: Cosmic time at which $\tau = 0$, any positive time; it fixes only the origin of $\tau$

coordinates.convention: We use the logarithmic time $\tau = t_0\ln(t/t_0)$, with $t$ the cosmic time, and the hyperbolic angle $\chi$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = c\tau$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{\tau}$ means $d(c\tau)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Inertial
coordinates.convention: We use the inertial coordinates of the comoving particle at $\chi = 0$, the time $T = t\cosh\chi$ and the distance $R = ct\sinh\chi$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = cT$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{T}$ means $d(cT)/d\lambda$.
